about: AI content audit of the timed bank (2026-10-13), incl. near-miss review.

bank-easy-01.note: Well-known right-sided filling causes; tamponade plus constrictive pericarditis make the link quick but it is accurate.

replacements.why: Causes lower-body edema but the jugular veins drain via the SVC, so JVP is not raised
Edema and ascites come from portal hypertension and low albumin; JVP is normal or low
Edema from hypoalbuminemia without raised central venous pressure

bank-easy-02.note: Macrolides, fluoroquinolones and antipsychotics together are the textbook QT list and are recognised instantly.

revision.why: Antipsychotics is the most reflexive QT member; ondansetron is a well-established, commonly tested QT-prolonging drug that requires recall.
revision.changes: Replace Antipsychotics with Ondansetron

replacements.why: A beta-blocker without sotalol's class III potassium-channel block, so it does not prolong QT
A tetracycline antibiotic not associated with QT prolongation
A class IB antiarrhythmic that shortens rather than prolongs the QT interval

bank-easy-03.note: Sarcoidosis and Crohn disease are the stock noncaseating examples, so the link comes quickly.

replacements.why: Forms necrotizing granulomas with vasculitis, not noncaseating granulomas
Produces stellate necrotizing (suppurative) granulomas
Forms fibrotic silicotic nodules rather than the noncaseating granulomas of berylliosis

bank-easy-06.note: Classic clubbing causes; quick for most students.

replacements.why: An acute infection; clubbing needs chronic suppuration such as abscess or bronchiectasis
An acute vascular event that does not cause clubbing

bank-easy-07.note: Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy are the two leading causes and give the link away quickly.

replacements.why: PTH rises in response to low or low-normal calcium, as in CKD, so calcium is not high
Secretes calcitonin, yet serum calcium stays normal
Phosphate release precipitates calcium, causing hypocalcemia

bank-easy-08.note: Standard hypokalemia causes; insulin adds a small shift-mechanism step.

replacements.why: A potassium-sparing ENaC blocker that raises serum potassium
Blocks ENaC like amiloride and causes hyperkalemia
Depolarization releases potassium from muscle, causing hyperkalemia
Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition causes hyperkalemia

bank-easy-09.note: Core nephrotic list from Step 1 review; recognised quickly.

replacements.why: Usually presents with episodic hematuria, a nephritic pattern
Type IV collagen defect causing hematuria, a nephritic pattern, with deafness
Causes pauci-immune crescentic, nephritic-pattern glomerulonephritis
A podocytopathy presenting with nephrotic syndrome
Causes progressive proteinuria in a nephrotic pattern, not an active nephritic sediment
A tubulointerstitial process with WBC casts, not glomerular inflammation

bank-easy-11.note: Three classic interstitial lung diseases plus IPF; the restrictive link is quick.

replacements.why: Permanent airway dilation that produces an obstructive pattern
Causes panacinar emphysema, an obstructive disease
Mucus plugging and bronchiectasis give an obstructive pattern

bank-easy-13.note: Gallstones and alcohol are the two causes every student names first, so the group sorts instantly.

revision.why: Alcohol use is the most reflexive member; azathioprine is a well-documented, commonly tested drug cause of acute pancreatitis.
revision.changes: Replace Alcohol use with Azathioprine

replacements.why: Pancreatic iron deposition causes diabetes, not acute pancreatitis
A cholestatic autoimmune liver disease that is not a cause of acute pancreatitis
A metabolic abnormality like hypertriglyceridemia but not a recognised trigger of pancreatitis

bank-easy-15.note: All four tiles start with T and come straight from the '5 Ts' mnemonic, so they sort with no reasoning.

revision.why: Breaks the all-T pattern from the mnemonic; hypoplastic left heart syndrome and pulmonary atresia are both standard, unambiguously cyanotic lesions.
revision.changes: Replace Truncus arteriosus with Hypoplastic left heart syndrome and Tricuspid atresia with Pulmonary atresia

replacements.why: An acyanotic left-to-right shunt (AV canal), classically seen in Down syndrome
An acyanotic lesion that leads to aortic stenosis later in life
An obstructive lesion that is acyanotic without an associated shunt

bank-medium-03.note: Three tiles end in '2', matching the 'MAD 2s' mnemonic, so the group sorts by format; the near misses (D1, H2, V2) partly counter this.

revision.why: Reduces the '2' pattern; the μ-opioid receptor is a certain, high-yield Gi-coupled receptor.
revision.changes: Replace D2 receptor with μ-opioid receptor

replacements.why: Couples to Gs, raising cAMP
Couples to Gq, raising IP3 and calcium
Couples to Gq, raising IP3 and calcium
Couples to Gq, unlike Gs-coupled V2

bank-medium-04.note: A numbered cranial nerve series from a memorised list; CN V2 and the internal carotid also traverse the sinus but are omitted.

revision.why: Breaks the pure CN-number series and adds the commonly forgotten but certain contents (ICA, V2).
revision.changes: Replace CN IV with Internal carotid artery and CN V1 with CN V2

replacements.why: Arises from the internal carotid after it leaves the sinus and enters the orbit via the optic canal
Enters the skull through foramen spinosum, lateral to the sinus
Lies above the sella, superomedial to the cavernous sinus, not within it

bank-medium-05.note: Memorised mnemonic list; all tiles end in 'artery', but so do the near misses, so it does not give the group away.

replacements.why: An inconstant vessel arising from the brachiocephalic trunk or aortic arch
A branch of the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian
A branch of the ophthalmic artery, from the internal carotid system

bank-medium-07.note: Needs embryology recall and discrimination (thyroid follicular vs parafollicular, spleen vs foregut organs).

replacements.why: Derived from neural crest, unlike endodermal follicular cells
Derived from neural crest
Derived from surface ectoderm, unlike the endodermal submandibular and sublingual glands

bank-medium-08.note: Core murmur timing; quick for most once paired with the diastolic group.

replacements.why: An early diastolic decrescendo murmur, often from pulmonary hypertension
Produces a diastolic pericardial knock, not a systolic murmur
Produces a friction rub, not a valvular systolic murmur

bank-medium-09.note: The complete set of semilunar regurgitation plus AV stenosis lesions, so the group is systematic; the near misses use the same format, which helps.

replacements.why: A systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur that increases with Valsalva
A midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur
A holosystolic murmur that increases with inspiration

bank-medium-10.note: Aortic regurgitation and PDA point quickly to bounding pulses; exercise requires a moment of physiology.

replacements.why: Raises peripheral resistance, causing diastolic hypertension and a narrowed pulse pressure
Limits LV filling and stroke volume, so pulse pressure is not widened
Restricted filling lowers stroke volume and narrows pulse pressure

bank-medium-11.note: Tamponade gives it away, but the other three need reasoning about intrathoracic pressure swings.

replacements.why: Produces an irregularly irregular pulse, not a respiratory drop in systolic pressure
Causes radiofemoral delay and arm-leg pressure differences, not pulsus paradoxus
IgA immune complexes with normal serum complement
A pauci-immune ANCA vasculitis with normal complement
Subepithelial immune deposits but serum complement is typically normal

bank-medium-13.note: Quick recall; 'Parasitic infection' is loose because protozoa such as Giardia and malaria typically do not cause eosinophilia.

revision.why: Eosinophilia is a feature of helminths, not protozoa; the standard term is more accurate.
revision.changes: Parasitic infection -> Helminth infection

replacements.why: A protozoan infection that does not cause eosinophilia
A protozoan infection that typically does not cause eosinophilia
Excess cortisol causes eosinopenia

bank-medium-14.note: Standard metabolic alkalosis causes; vomiting and diuretics make it quick.

replacements.why: Causes respiratory alkalosis, not metabolic alkalosis
Impaired H+ secretion causes a non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
Causes respiratory alkalosis plus anion-gap metabolic acidosis, not metabolic alkalosis

bank-medium-15.note: Requires linking each to hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance; good mechanism group.

replacements.why: Causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and can cause distal (type 1) RTA, not type 4
Light chains cause proximal tubular damage and Fanconi syndrome (type 2 RTA)
Carbonic anhydrase inhibition causes proximal bicarbonate wasting, not hyperkalemic type 4 RTA

bank-hard-01.note: Each name is strongly tied to 'body', but many other eponymous bodies exist (Mallory, Councilman, Negri), which suits a wordplay round.

replacements.why: Auer rods, not bodies, in acute myeloid leukemia
Charcot-Leyden crystals, not bodies, from eosinophils
Reed-Sternberg cells, not bodies, in Hodgkin lymphoma
Curschmann spirals, not bodies, in asthma

bank-hard-02.note: Beck and Charcot triads are well known; Virchow and Whipple deliberately overlap with node and disease eponyms.

replacements.why: Kussmaul sign and Kussmaul breathing, not a triad
Courvoisier sign (palpable nontender gallbladder), not a triad
Cullen sign (periumbilical bruising), not a triad

bank-hard-03.note: Heberden and Bouchard are a fixed pair, so the group is quick once one is spotted.

replacements.why: Janeway lesions (painless palmar macules), not nodes, in endocarditis
Gottron papules, not nodes, in dermatomyositis
Roth spots, not nodes, in endocarditis

bank-hard-04.note: Well-known eponymous spots; quick for most.

replacements.why: Janeway lesions, not spots, in endocarditis
Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), not spots, in NF1
Kayser-Fleischer rings, not spots, in Wilson disease
Osler nodes, not spots, in endocarditis

bank-hard-05.note: 'Kerley B' almost spells out 'lines'; the others need more thought.

replacements.why: Wickham striae, not lines, in lichen planus
Terry nails, not lines, in cirrhosis
Lindsay (half-and-half) nails, not lines, in chronic kidney disease

bank-hard-06.note: Very well-known signs, though dozens of other eponymous signs exist, so the group relies on excluding other eponym categories.

replacements.why: Argyll Robertson pupil, not sign, in neurosyphilis
Austin Flint murmur, not sign, in aortic regurgitation
Janeway lesions, not sign, in endocarditis

bank-hard-07.note: Arthus is standardly called the Arthus reaction, so it fits 'phenomenon' less cleanly than the others.

revision.why: Uhthoff phenomenon (heat-induced worsening in MS) is a certain, standard 'phenomenon' eponym, unlike the usual 'Arthus reaction'.
revision.changes: Replace Arthus with Uhthoff

replacements.why: Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding on scale removal), not phenomenon, in psoriasis
Gowers sign (using hands to rise from the floor), not phenomenon, in Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Nikolsky sign, not phenomenon, in pemphigus vulgaris

bank-hard-08.note: 'Vein', 'hypertension' and 'triad' converge on 'portal' quickly; 'triad' usefully overlaps with the eponymous-triad group.

replacements.why: The liver's arterial supply is the hepatic artery; there is no 'portal artery'
Hepatic sinusoids receive portal blood, but 'portal sinusoid' is not a standard term

bank-hard-11.note: Three tiles start with 'Stellate' and one with 'Starry', so the group sorts with no medical knowledge.

revision.why: Keeps the star theme (astro- means star) but removes the repeated 'Stellate' stem; asteroid bodies (star-shaped inclusions in sarcoid giant cells) and astrocytes are standard, certain terms.
revision.changes: Replace Stellate cells with Astrocytes and Stellate ganglion with Asteroid bodies

replacements.why: Named after the moon, not a star, in Cushing syndrome
Named after the sun, not a star, in osteosarcoma
Named for the crescent moon shape, not a star, in RPGN

bank-expert-01.note: All tiles start with 'Hyper-' while the paired group all start with 'Hypo-', so players sort by prefix alone; also nearly every hyper- state lowers some value (e.g., hyperthyroidism lowers TSH), so membership is not unique.

bank-expert-02.note: All tiles start with 'Hypo-', so the group sorts by prefix alone; nearly every hypo- state raises some value (e.g., primary adrenal insufficiency raises ACTH), so membership is not unique.

bank-expert-03.note: Good feedback reasoning, but the title also fits endogenous excess (Graves disease, cortisol-secreting adenoma) while all tiles are exogenous.

revision.title: Exogenous hormone that suppresses its own upstream signal
revision.why: All four members are exogenous; the narrower title excludes endogenous hormone-excess diseases that would otherwise also fit.
revision.changes: Add 'Exogenous' to the title

replacements.why: Blocks hypothalamic estrogen feedback, so LH and FSH rise rather than fall
Blocks thyroid hormone synthesis, so TSH rises rather than being suppressed
Inhibits steroid synthesis, so ACTH rises rather than being suppressed
An upstream GnRH agonist that suppresses downstream LH/FSH by receptor downregulation, not a downstream hormone feeding back

bank-expert-05.note: 'Insulin resistance' repeats the title's 'resistant'; the other three need recognising end-organ resistance.

revision.why: Removes the title leak; Laron syndrome (GH receptor defect with high GH and low IGF-1) is a certain, Step 1-tested example of hormone resistance.
revision.changes: Replace Insulin resistance with Laron syndrome

replacements.why: Shares the Albright phenotype but has normal PTH and normal end-organ response
ACTH is high because cortisol output fails, not because tissues resist ACTH
TSH is high because the gland fails, not because of TSH resistance

bank-expert-06.note: Strong cross-system idea, but many diseases have some value that falls (e.g., hemoglobin and albumin fall in multiple myeloma), so the title needs narrowing to severity-defining organ-function measures (GFR, EF, FEV1, FVC/DLCO).

revision.title: Severity staged by a falling organ-function measure
revision.why: Each member's severity is formally staged by a falling functional measure (GFR, EF, FEV1, FVC/DLCO); the current title also admits diseases like multiple myeloma.
revision.changes: Narrow the title to staging by an organ-function measure

replacements.why: Tracked by serum urate, which rises with disease
Graded by BMI, which rises as disease worsens
Graded by wall thickness and outflow gradient, which rise; ejection fraction is typically preserved

bank-neuro-01.note: Classic neuropathy causes; vincristine adds a pharmacology step but the group is quick.

replacements.why: A presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder, not peripheral nerve damage
A chemotherapy agent known for cardiotoxicity, not neuropathy like vincristine
Blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, without nerve damage

bank-neuro-02.note: CN III/IV/VI palsy is a numbered series with a repeated 'palsy' stem; the mimic near misses are strong.

revision.why: Breaks the CN III/IV/VI series; internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion) is a certain, high-yield lesion localised on eye exam.
revision.changes: Replace CN IV palsy with Internuclear ophthalmoplegia

replacements.why: Ptosis and ophthalmoplegia from blocked acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, not a nerve lesion
A benign pupil asymmetry with no ptosis and no neural lesion, unlike Horner syndrome

bank-neuro-03.note: Standard cord syndromes; quick for most, with good look-alike near misses.

replacements.why: A brainstem stroke of the anterior spinal artery territory in the medulla, not the cord
A chronic peripheral demyelinating neuropathy, not a cord lesion
Compression of a single nerve root, outside the spinal cord

bank-neuro-04.note: Requires tracing each pathway's decussation; the shared word 'lesion' also appears in near misses so it does not sort.

replacements.why: Pyramid is damaged above the decussation, so weakness is contralateral
Causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia
Midbrain cerebral peduncle lesion above the decussation gives contralateral weakness
Sensory pathways have already crossed, so loss is contralateral

bank-migrated-sys-mixed-0001-L1.note: Place names are recognizable on sight; tile 4 is a virus rather than a disease, slightly mismatching the title.

replacements.why: Named for 'query' (unknown cause), not a place
Severe leptospirosis named after Adolf Weil, a person
Leprosy named after Gerhard Hansen, a person

bank-migrated-sys-mixed-0001-L2.note: Classic 'I 8 10 eggs at 12' recall; thoracic duct, azygos vein and phrenic nerve also pass through.

replacements.why: Arises from the abdominal aorta below the diaphragm and never crosses it
Lies entirely within the abdomen
An aortic arch branch going to the arm, staying above the diaphragm
Run from the lungs to the left atrium entirely within the thorax

bank-migrated-sys-mixed-0001-L3.note: Standard fetal circulation list; umbilical arteries (medial umbilical ligaments) fit equally well.

replacements.why: Embryologic duct whose remnant is the foramen cecum/pyramidal lobe, not circulatory
Becomes the round ligament or gubernaculum testis, not a circulatory structure
Forms the ductus deferens and related ducts, not a circulatory structure

bank-migrated-sys-mixed-0001-L4.note: Well-known thrombophilia list; mixing gene variants with syndromes keeps it from being purely format-based.

replacements.why: Autoimmune platelet destruction causing bleeding, not clotting
GpIIb/IIIa deficiency causing a platelet aggregation bleeding disorder
Factor IX deficiency causing bleeding
Hemophilia C, a bleeding tendency rather than thrombophilia

bank-migrated-sys-micro-0001-L1.note: A recognized acid-fast list, but mixing bacteria and protozoa takes a moment of recall.

replacements.why: Identified by India ink or mucicarmine staining, not acid-fast
Seen with silver stain; it is not acid-fast
An apicomplexan like Cryptosporidium, but not identified by acid-fast staining

bank-migrated-sys-micro-0001-L3.note: Classic spirochete list (Borrelia, Leptospira, Treponema); two Borrelia tiles help.

replacements.why: A spiral rat-bite fever bacterium with polar flagella, not a spirochete
Transmitted by Ixodes ticks like B. burgdorferi, but a rickettsial organism
Louse-borne like B. recurrentis, but a rickettsia, not a spirochete

bank-migrated-sys-micro-0001-L4.note: Standard list; Coxiella can now be grown axenically, though it is still taught as obligate intracellular.

replacements.why: Facultative intracellular; can be cultured on cysteine-enriched media
Facultative intracellular and grows in culture
Survives in macrophages but is facultative and grows on Lowenstein-Jensen medium

bank-migrated-sys-mixed-0002-L1.note: McBurney's point makes the group instant, and psoas/obturator signs are the textbook companions.

replacements.why: Right subscapular hyperesthesia in acute cholecystitis
Empty right lower quadrant in intussusception
Pain persists with tensed abdominal wall, pointing to an abdominal wall source
Palpable painless gallbladder with jaundice, suggesting pancreatic head cancer

bank-migrated-sys-mixed-0002-L2.note: Kernig and Brudzinski are instant pairs; jolt accentuation adds a little difficulty.

replacements.why: Neck extension and rotation reproduces radicular pain in cervical radiculopathy
Straight leg raise tests lumbosacral nerve root irritation, not meninges
A sign of raised intracranial pressure, not meningeal irritation

bank-migrated-sys-biochem-0001-L1.note: Four of the most-quoted autosomal dominant examples.

replacements.why: A trinucleotide repeat disorder like Huntington, but autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive HFE mutation
X-linked, not autosomal

bank-migrated-sys-biochem-0001-L2.note: Classic autosomal recessive examples; quick for most students.

replacements.why: Adult polycystic kidney disease is autosomal dominant
Usually autosomal dominant
Autosomal dominant FGFR3 mutation
A lysosomal storage disease like Tay-Sachs, but X-linked
X-linked dominant MECP2 disorder, seen almost only in girls
Autosomal recessive, unlike X-linked Hunter syndrome
Factor XI deficiency is autosomal recessive

bank-migrated-sys-hemeonc-0001-L1.note: Acute/chronic x lymphoid/myeloid grid with 'leukemia' in every tile; sorts with no reasoning, consider retiring.

replacements.why: Reactive benign leukocytosis, not a leukemia
Immature cells in blood from marrow infiltration, not a leukemia
A clonal marrow disorder that can progress to AML but is not itself a leukemia
A myeloproliferative neoplasm, not a leukemia

bank-migrated-sys-hemeonc-0001-L2.note: The t(x;y) notation sorts them instantly unless near misses also use translocation notation.

replacements.why: EWSR1-FLI1 translocation of Ewing sarcoma, a bone tumor, not a blood cancer
SS18-SSX translocation of synovial sarcoma, not a blood cancer
A numeric change seen in CLL, not a translocation
A deletion seen in myelodysplastic syndrome, not a translocation

bank-migrated-sys-hemeonc-0001-L3.note: Two 'CA' tiles flag the group, but AFP and CEA are equally familiar.

replacements.why: Falls in intravascular hemolysis; not a tumor marker
Marker of fibrin breakdown in thrombosis or DIC, not cancer
Marker of pancreatitis, not pancreatic cancer
Marker of myocardial injury

bank-migrated-sys-hemeonc-0001-L4.note: Must separate leukemia findings from other classic smear findings shown alongside them.

replacements.why: Bilobed neutrophils of Pelger-Huet anomaly or myelodysplasia, not a leukemia finding
Classic for lead poisoning and thalassemia
Denatured hemoglobin in G6PD deficiency

bank-migrated-sys-pharm-0001-L1.note: Famous mnemonic, but mydriasis and confusion also fit sympathomimetic and serotonergic near misses.

replacements.why: Characteristic of serotonin syndrome, not anticholinergic toxicity
Characteristic of neuroleptic malignant syndrome
A sign of opioid withdrawal
A cholinergic (muscarinic) sign

bank-migrated-sys-pharm-0001-L2.note: SSRIs and MAOIs are obvious; tramadol and linezolid add recall.

replacements.why: An opioid without meaningful serotonergic activity, unlike tramadol
An MRSA antibiotic like linezolid but with no monoamine oxidase inhibition
Treats malignant hyperthermia; it does not raise serotonin

bank-migrated-sys-pharm-0001-L3.note: Famous antidotes, though near misses linked to the same toxins make it fair.

replacements.why: A partial opioid agonist used for opioid use disorder, not to reverse overdose
A cholinesterase inhibitor for myasthenia that does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so not used to reverse anticholinergic delirium
A muscarinic agonist for urinary retention, not an antidote

bank-migrated-sys-mixed-0003-L1.note: All four tiles start with T, matching the '5 Ts' mnemonic, so they sort on the first letter alone.

revision.why: Swapping two of the 5-T lesions for two other definitely cyanotic lesions removes the T giveaway while keeping the group correct.
revision.changes: Truncus arteriosus -> Hypoplastic left heart syndrome; Tricuspid atresia -> Pulmonary atresia

replacements.why: Left-to-right shunt, acyanotic at presentation (Down syndrome association)
L-TGA is physiologically corrected and acyanotic without other lesions
Acyanotic valve lesion

bank-migrated-sys-mixed-0003-L2.note: Needs recall of arch versus pouch and cleft derivatives, which the near misses test.

replacements.why: Arises from the floor of the pharynx at the foramen cecum, not a pharyngeal arch
Derived from the 1st pharyngeal pouch
Derived from the 4th pouch (ultimobranchial body)

bank-migrated-sys-mixed-0003-L3.note: Spells the TORCH acronym directly; congenital syphilis (the 'O') is an equally expected member.

replacements.why: Causes ophthalmia neonatorum acquired at delivery; not a TORCH agent
Causes neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia; not a TORCH agent
A cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis, not a TORCH agent

bank-migrated-sys-mixed-0003-L4.note: Familiar defects, but near misses with Chiari and Dandy-Walker require discrimination.

replacements.why: Hemispheres are destroyed and replaced by fluid within an intact skull; not a closure defect
Premature fusion of skull sutures, not a neural tube defect
Sacral agenesis linked to maternal diabetes, not failed neural tube closure

bank-migrated-sys-cardio-0001-L1.note: Core murmur timing; quick but requires separating from diastolic look-alikes.

replacements.why: Diastolic murmur at the left lower sternal border
Mid-diastolic rumble from severe aortic regurgitation
Early diastolic murmur of pulmonic regurgitation in pulmonary hypertension

bank-migrated-sys-cardio-0001-L2.note: Core murmur timing; Austin Flint adds a little recall.

replacements.why: Holosystolic murmur
Holosystolic murmur that increases with inspiration
Systolic ejection murmur

bank-migrated-sys-cardio-0001-L3.note: Requires Carvallo reasoning, but tricuspid regurgitation, the most classic example, is missing and players will expect it.

replacements.why: Left-sided; louder with expiration and leaning forward
Left-sided diastolic rumble that does not augment with inspiration
A septal shunt murmur, not right-sided valve disease

bank-migrated-sys-cardio-0001-L4.note: Three tiles end in 'wave'; 'named waveform' is loose, as U waves or Wellens T waves could also be argued in.

replacements.why: A named polymorphic VT rhythm, not a single-beat waveform finding
A named conduction pattern across beats, not a waveform
A named aberrant conduction pattern in atrial fibrillation, not a waveform

bank-migrated-sys-cardio-0002-L1.note: Pump failure causes are familiar; discrimination comes from obstructive and distributive near misses.

replacements.why: Obstructive shock; the RV outflow is blocked
Distributive shock from loss of sympathetic tone
Distributive and hypovolemic shock from cortisol deficiency

bank-migrated-sys-cardio-0002-L2.note: Classic obstructive causes; constrictive pericarditis usually causes chronic low output more than frank shock.

replacements.why: Cardiogenic shock from impaired contractility
Cardiogenic shock from an ineffective rhythm
Distributive shock from loss of sympathetic tone
Shock from cortisol deficiency, not mechanical obstruction

bank-migrated-sys-cardio-0002-L3.note: Requires reasoning about left atrial pressure against pre-capillary near misses.

replacements.why: Right heart failure from lung disease with a normal wedge pressure
Lowers filling pressures, including the wedge
Distributive shock with a low or normal wedge pressure

bank-migrated-sys-cardio-0003-L1.note: Well-known causes; the hypo/hyperthyroid near miss adds a small trap.

replacements.why: A beta-2 agonist that causes tachycardia
Causes compensatory tachycardia
Catecholamine excess causes tachycardia

bank-migrated-sys-cardio-0003-L2.note: Familiar SVTs; antidromic AVRT near miss rewards real discrimination.

replacements.why: Chaotic ventricular activity with no organized narrow QRS
Ventricular pacing produces wide paced complexes

bank-migrated-sys-cardio-0003-L3.note: First, second (I and II) and third degree form an obvious series, with 'AV block' in title and tiles.

replacements.why: A block between the sinus node and atrium, not at the AV node
An intraventricular fascicular block, not AV block

bank-migrated-sys-cardio-0003-L4.note: Mixed tile types require reasoning; hypokalemia, the most classic risk factor, is missing.

replacements.why: Causes peaked T waves and conduction block, not QT prolongation
Shortens QT; associated with bidirectional VT rather than torsades
A congenital channelopathy with short repolarization, not torsades risk
Class IB agent that shortens repolarization

bank-migrated-sys-pulm-0001-L2.note: Classic restrictive versus obstructive split; mixing parenchymal and chest wall causes adds a little.

replacements.why: Predominantly obstructive airway disease
Causes panacinar emphysema, an obstructive pattern
Small airway obstruction, an obstructive pattern

bank-migrated-sys-pulm-0001-L3.note: Requires reasoning about surface area, membrane, capillary volume and hemoglobin.

replacements.why: Chest wall restriction with a normal alveolar membrane, so DLCO is preserved
DLCO is normal or increased
Increased pulmonary blood flow raises DLCO

bank-migrated-sys-pulm-0001-L4.note: Uncommonly taught direction of DLCO change that requires mechanistic reasoning; asthma and obesity can also raise DLCO.

replacements.why: Carboxyhemoglobin back pressure lowers measured DLCO
Reduced capillary blood volume lowers DLCO
Interstitial involvement lowers DLCO

bank-migrated-sys-pulm-0002-L1.note: Standard transudate list driven by Starling forces.

replacements.why: Produces a lymphocyte-rich exudate
Serositis produces an exudate
Produces an exudate with high amylase and low pH

bank-migrated-sys-pulm-0002-L2.note: Pulmonary embolism produces transudates in a meaningful minority, so it is a loose member.

revision.why: Pulmonary embolism effusions can be transudates; acute pancreatitis reliably causes an exudate.
revision.changes: Pulmonary embolism -> Acute pancreatitis

replacements.why: Low oncotic pressure produces a transudate
Lowered pleural pressure produces a transudate
Raised venous pressure produces a transudate

bank-migrated-sys-pulm-0002-L3.note: Classic upper-zone list; sarcoidosis, ankylosing spondylitis, cystic fibrosis and centriacinar emphysema also fit and may be expected.

replacements.why: The Ghon focus is typically in the mid or lower lung zones, unlike reactivation disease.
Thin-walled cysts are diffuse and uniform, without the upper-zone, base-sparing pattern of PLCH.
NSIP pattern that is basal predominant.
Favor the lung bases, where blood flow is greatest.

bank-migrated-sys-pulm-0002-L4.note: Sound pairing with the upper-lobe set; aspiration location depends on posture (posterior upper-lobe segments when supine), so it needs an unstated exception.

replacements.why: Perilymphatic nodules favor the upper and mid zones.
Bronchiectasis is upper-lobe predominant.
